<meta>continues from previous page: the sentence concerns what to do if a consort of the described qualities is not available.</meta>
...if there is none. In that case one should bring in a woman in whom youthfulness predominates, whoever can be found, for this way of the <term>yoginī</term> <gloss>female yogic partner</gloss> is the way of great passion. With this the characteristics of the disciple have been shown in brief.

Now, in order to show the secret consecration in brief, the text says "As long as..." and so on. "The face of the seal, too": this means the face of the disciple. "Of the means": this means of the disciple. In "One should do the act..." and so on, "to that very one, too" means to the wisdom consort. "Equal taste" refers to the wisdom consecration. "The disciple's field of experience" means that the disciple's blindfold is removed.

What comes about through these? To answer, the text says "Self-aware..." and so on: through equal taste of exactly that kind, it becomes self-aware gnosis itself. Of what particular character is this? To answer, the text says "Self and other..." and so on: it is free from discriminating into the portions of self and other. "Equal to space" means equal to the sky, because it is without appearance. It is "stainless" because it is without afflictions. It is "empty" because it has wholly passed beyond conceptual elaboration. "Existence" is arising; "non-existence" is cessation. That which is the nature of both is spoken of in this way.

"Supreme" means ultimate wisdom. The emptiness that belongs with the means is wisdom. The means is great compassion, which is to experience fully all sentient beings as equal to oneself. Their "mingling" means that they come to appear as a single form. "Passion" is supreme joy. "Free of passion" is the joy of the absence of joy <note>the "joy of cessation", one of the four joys of tantric practice</note>; it is the nature in which these become mingled.

"Living beings" means sentient beings. They themselves are the life, because without them there would be no life. "The supreme syllable": this is because it has the form of the <term>dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>the sphere of reality</gloss>, without beginning or end. "The pervader": this is because all phenomena have it as their nature. "It abides in all bodies": this is because consciousness abides in the bodies of living beings. From that very one, beings...

<summary>This page of a tantric commentary explains the choice of consort for the disciple and then glosses, phrase by phrase, a root-text passage on the secret consecration. It describes the resulting self-aware gnosis as beyond self and other, like space, stainless, empty, and a union of wisdom and compassion that pervades all beings.</summary>
<keywords>secret consecration, wisdom consecration, yoginī, consort, disciple, blindfold, self-aware gnosis, emptiness, great compassion, supreme joy, joy of cessation, dharmadhātu, supreme syllable, tantric commentary, Tibetan Tengyur</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the page opens at the end of a mantra being quoted.</meta>
...<term>na tvāt oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā</term> <note>the closing syllables of a Sanskrit mantra, left in transliteration</note>; that is how it goes. "Making offerings and supplications" means to the guru. "Just as it has been taught" means as in the <term>Tattvasaṃgraha</term> <gloss>Compendium of Reality, a major yoga tantra</gloss> and similar works. "Vajrasattva" means Hevajra. "Afterwards" means immediately following the consecration.

"Purified" means that the faults of cyclic existence are purified. "Having the form of gnosis" means equal to the gnosis of omniscience. In "Saṃsāra and purification...", the words "that gnosis in which existence and nirvāṇa have not the slightest difference" are to be supplied; the intended sense is "because it has wholly passed beyond all conceptual elaboration." This very point will be shown clearly by the two verses beginning "In supreme joy..."

"Supreme joy" is the wisdom that has become supreme, the gnosis characterized by clear light. "There is no meditation there" means there is nothing whatsoever to be meditated upon. The meditator is the mind, and that too does not exist. "Body" means the body. "The grasped" is the object that comes to appear. "The grasper" is the eye and the other senses. In the same way, flesh, blood and the rest do not exist either.

Having thus established that the obscuration of the afflictions does not exist, the text goes on with "There is no seeing..." and so on, to show that the obscuration of the knowable does not exist either. The meaning is that external things, such as what is to be seen, do not exist either.

In "without waves..." and so on, "waves" are conceptual thoughts. Their exhaustion is "without waves." "Variety" is appearing in a variety of forms; its absence is "without variety."

"Thus" means: thus spoke the Blessed One. "Asked" means that Vajragarbha made a request. What did he ask? The text says "Why..." and so on. The intention is this: of what is purified by its own nature, the essence of the innate...

<summary>The commentary glosses verses following the consecration, identifying Vajrasattva with Hevajra and describing the purified gnosis in which saṃsāra and nirvāṇa do not differ. It explains that in supreme joy there is no meditator, nothing meditated, no grasper or grasped, so that both afflictive and cognitive obscurations are absent, and introduces Vajragarbha's question.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra, Vajrasattva, Vajragarbha, consecration, mantra, Tattvasaṃgraha, gnosis, clear light, supreme joy, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, obscuration of afflictions, obscuration of the knowable, conceptual thought, innate, tantric commentary</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the commentator has just said that the following is to be sung as a song.</meta>
...and it is to be sung as a song. That song is the one beginning "<term>mala aje</term>" and so on. <note>What follows glosses, word by word, a song in Apabhraṃśa, a vernacular form of Indic language, transmitted in Tibetan transliteration. The Apabhraṃśa words are kept as terms and the commentator's explanations translated.</note>

<term>Kolla iri</term> means the head. <term>Bolla</term> is the syllable <term>haṃ</term> that abides there. <term>Mummuni</term> means the view. <term>Kakkolā</term> is the syllable <term>aṃ</term>. The union of those two is <term>ghaṇa</term> <gloss>dense</gloss>, that is, uninterrupted. <term>Kripiṭā</term> is the indestructible sound. <term>Bājja</term> means that this arises everywhere. <term>Kāruṇi</term> means the yogin. <term>Ka a i</term> means "does not do." <term>Ṇarola</term> means that he does not engage in external union. <term>Tahiṃ bila</term> means one's own being. <term>Khajja i</term> means that one should make oneself unobservable. <term>Ma a ṇa bija a i</term> means that one should drink the drink of great bliss born from yoga. <term>Kaliñja</term> is the wind. <term>Pani a i</term> means by entering within. <term>Dudhura</term> means the afflictions, such as passion. <term>Ca u sama</term> is the aggregate of form. <term>Kacchuri</term> is feeling. <term>Sihla</term> is perception. <term>Kapura</term> is consciousness. <term>Lā i a i</term> means "joins together." <term>Mala indhaṇa</term> is the aggregate of formations. All of these together, whose nature is pride in a self, are <term>sālija</term>.

<term>Tahaṃ</term>: there the yogin is to eat them, which means they are to be made without inherent nature. <term>Phreṃkhaṇa kheṭa</term>: the descent of the <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>the mind of awakening, here the vital fluid</gloss> from great bliss is called <term>phreṃkhaṇa</term>, and its entering back again is called <term>kheṭa</term>. <term>Śuddha aśuddha</term> means not knowing <note>that is, not conceiving</note> existence and non-existence. For that very reason, <term>niraṃsu</term>: because it accords with that, it is <term>niraṃsu</term>, the drop of fluid. By that, <term>aṃbha</term> means it is to be placed in the channels of the limbs of the body. <term>Tahiṃ</term> means by a union of that kind. <term>Sarāva</term> is <term>Nairātmyā</term> <gloss>the goddess Selflessness</gloss>, the selflessness of all phenomena. <term>Paṇi a i</term> means "is to be followed." <term>Malayaja</term> means the gathering of the channels.

<summary>The commentator explains a vernacular Apabhraṃśa song word by word, reading its everyday images as a code for yogic practice. The words stand for the syllables haṃ and aṃ, the inner winds, the five aggregates, the descent and return of the bodhicitta through the channels, and the goddess Nairātmyā.</summary>
<keywords>Apabhraṃśa song, vajra song, Hevajra, syllable haṃ, syllable aṃ, unstruck sound, great bliss, five aggregates, bodhicitta, channels, wind, Nairātmyā, selflessness, yogin, tantric commentary</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the sentence warns the practitioner about intoxication.</meta>
...the yogin who does this should not become intoxicated, for if delusion predominates it becomes a great obstacle to yoga. One should train in this way.

This concludes the commentary on the sixth chapter, the chapter on conduct, from the <term>Yogaratnamālā</term> <gloss>Jewel Garland of Yoga</gloss>, the difficult-point commentary on the Hevajra.

***

"Signs" are a foreign tongue, a showing of signs understood by the <term>yoginīs</term> <gloss>female practitioners</gloss>. It should be understood that this is itself a supreme means. Therefore the text says "Then the chapter on signs..." and so on; this is also said of the chapter that makes the signs clear.

"Brother" means a yogin. "Sister" means a yoginī. "One finger" means the index finger; the meaning is "Have you come?" "Whoever" means whoever should look. "With two" means with the index and middle fingers. "Showing a hanging banner" means showing with those two the manner of a tied, hanging silk banner. "Three-pointed" means that the little finger is pressed down by the thumb and the rest are stretched out in the manner of three points. "Boundary" means the boundary at the crown of the head. "Wheel" means showing the gesture of a wheel. "Frown" means moving the eyebrows. "Untying the topknot" and the rest are an explanation in the provisional sense <note>that is, a meaning that needs further interpretation, as opposed to the definitive sense given next</note>.

In "Showing one finger..." and so on: "one finger," the index finger, or the middle and index fingers together, is shown at the lotus of the wisdom consort, that is, she is to be stimulated. In "That itself has come well," "well" means the fluid; the meaning is that it has been brought down by joining the fingers.

In "In the seal of illness..." and so on, the "seal of illness" is the full accomplishment of the <term>dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss> that is the culmination of bliss; it is knowing these. What is it like? The text says "From holding the left thumb..." and so on. "Left" means wisdom, that is, within her lotus. "Thumb" means the <term>vajra</term>; when by it the stage of flowing has been reached, it is to be pressed. In "The ring finger..." and so on, "ring finger" means the gnosis of wisdom...

<summary>This page closes the commentary on the sixth chapter, on conduct, of the Yogaratnamālā, a commentary on the Hevajra Tantra. It opens the seventh chapter on secret signs, explaining hand gestures by which yogins and yoginīs recognize each other, first in their outward sense and then in their inner yogic meaning.</summary>
<keywords>Yogaratnamālā, Hevajra Tantra, chapter on conduct, chapter on signs, secret signs, hand gestures, yogin, yoginī, provisional meaning, wisdom consort, lotus, vajra, dharmadhātu, bliss, tantric commentary</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the commentary is decoding a mantra given in the root text as a cipher, naming each letter by its row in the Sanskrit alphabet or by a goddess who stands for a vowel.</meta>
...is <term>pha</term>. The first of the third row is the letter <term>ṭa</term>. The fourth of the fifth row is <term>bha</term>. The first of the semivowels <note>literally "those standing at the end," the letters ya, ra, la, va that follow the five rows of stops</note> is <term>ya</term>. <term>Ghasmarī</term> is the letter <term>o</term>. The first of the first row is <term>ka</term>. The inner <term>Gaurī</term> is <term>i</term>. The first of the third row is <term>ṭa</term>. The third of the fifth row is <term>ba</term>. The third of the second row is <term>ja</term>. The first of the fourth row is <term>ta</term>. The fire-eater is the <term>repha</term> <gloss>the letter ra</gloss>. <term>Vetālī</term> is <term>e</term>. The third of the semivowels is <term>la</term>. The first of the first row is <term>ka</term>. The first of the semivowels is <term>ya</term>. <term>Vajrā</term> is <term>a</term>. <term>Caurī</term> is <term>ai</term>. The first of the fifth row is <term>pa</term>. <term>Nairātmyā</term> is <term>a</term>. The first of the first row is <term>ka</term>. The first of the second row is <term>ca</term>. The first of the third row is <term>ṭa</term>. The first of the fourth row is <term>ta</term>. The first of the fifth row is <term>pa</term>. The first of the semivowels is <term>ya</term>. The first of the sibilants <note>Sanskrit <term>ūṣman</term>, the "hot" letters</note> is <term>śa</term>. The second of the semivowels is <term>ra</term>. <term>Vajrā</term> is <term>a</term>.

This concludes the commentary on the ninth chapter of the second part, from the <term>Yogaratnamālā</term> <gloss>Jewel Garland of Yoga</gloss>, the difficult-point commentary on the Hevajra.

***

In "Then..." and so on: "the single vow" is the vow that is the condensed summary of non-duality. "Recitation" means mantra recitation. Its object is the rosary. "With buffalo" means with a rosary of buffalo bone. To show the pledges of the various ritual actions, the text says "For paralysing..." and so on; this is easy to understand.

This concludes the commentary on the tenth chapter of the second part, from the <term>Yogaratnamālā</term>, the difficult-point commentary on the Hevajra.

***

In "Close embrace..." and so on: "Thus" refers to what is about to be explained. "The family of Akṣobhya" means the family of that Akṣobhya. "The family of the mind" means the family of Vajrasattva. "These" means that those women belong to the <term>tathāgata</term> <gloss>buddha</gloss> families. "Made to Nairātmyā" is an invocation. "By intoxication" means that great bliss comes to arise. "Of the sign" means placing a fingernail mark for that purpose. "With the hand" means stirring with two fingers and the like. "Possessing the vajra"...

<summary>The page finishes decoding a mantra hidden in a letter cipher, where letters are named by their row and position in the Sanskrit alphabet or by goddesses standing for vowels. It then closes the commentaries on chapters nine and ten of the second part of the Hevajra Tantra in the Yogaratnamālā and begins the next chapter on the families of consorts and signs of union.</summary>
<keywords>Yogaratnamālā, Hevajra Tantra, mantra cipher, Sanskrit alphabet, letter rows, semivowels, sibilants, Ghasmarī, Gaurī, Vetālī, Caurī, Nairātmyā, Vajrā, rosary, buffalo bone, ritual actions, Akṣobhya, Vajrasattva, buddha families, great bliss</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: commentary on the Hevajra Tantra, explaining the visualization of the seed syllable and the emanation of the deity</meta>
"...is called the Being." This means that this very seed syllable is declared to be <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>the Vajra-Holder, the primordial buddha</gloss>. If one asks what its special character is, the text says: "It has the nature of supreme bliss." "One should emanate" means that from that very seed syllable one should send forth, pervading everything, a variety of forms all resembling the body of <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>the "Joyful Vajra" deity</gloss>.

"Having gathered them into the heart" means that one should gather all of them back together and dissolve them into that same seed syllable. Then the yogin, having become one whose very nature is wrath, is transformed into the form of <term>Heruka</term> <gloss>the wrathful tantric deity</gloss> through the complete transformation of the moon, the sun, the emblem, and the seed syllable. These are the five aspects of <term>abhisambodhi</term> <gloss>manifest awakening</gloss>.

As it says in the eighth chapter:

The moon possesses mirror-like wisdom;
The seventh of seven possesses the wisdom of sameness;
The seed syllable and emblem of the deity
Are said to be discriminating wisdom;
All becoming one is the wisdom of accomplishment;
The completed form is the purity of the <term>dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>the sphere of reality</gloss>.

<note>"The seventh of seven" is a cryptic name for the sun, which in Indian reckoning is associated with seven horses or the seventh day. Each of the five stages of visualization is matched with one of the five wisdoms of a buddha.</note>

The three verses beginning "Blue, and the sun" and so on describe the yoga of the solitary hero, which is common to all the deities.

Next, in order to teach in brief the fourth yoga, the yoga of <term>Nairātmyā</term> <gloss>the goddess "Selflessness," Hevajra's consort</gloss>, together with the four forms of Hevajra, whose nature is the wheel of the mandala, the text says "Charnel ground" and so on. Just as with the activity of the third yoga, the fourth should be viewed in the same way. Inside the vajra fence, within the palace of the mandala of the eight terrifying charnel grounds, the Lord Hevajra is surrounded by the eight yoginīs, Gaurī and the rest.

"Where the breath moves": this is an etymological gloss in which letters of the phrase "because it has become the abode of corpses" have been elided, so that it means "the abode of corpses." <note>The commentator is explaining a play on the Sanskrit word for charnel ground, śmaśāna, read as a contraction of a longer phrase.</note> By this word "charnel ground," a brief statement is made of the completion stage taught in the eighth chapter, which will be explained later. The "charnel ground" is the body of the selfless one, in which the Lord, whose nature is supreme bliss, dwells. If one asks how the body is a charnel ground, the text says:

By this reasoning, "where the breath moves,"
It is called a "charnel ground."

Now, in order to describe in particular the four-armed Hevajra,

<summary>This page of a Tibetan commentary on the Hevajra Tantra explains the dissolution of emanated deities into the seed syllable and the five stages of manifest awakening by which the yogin arises as Heruka, matched to the five wisdoms. It then introduces the fourth yoga, the mandala of Hevajra and Nairātmyā in the eight charnel grounds, and interprets the charnel ground as the yogin's own body.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, commentary, Vajradhara, Heruka, Nairātmyā, five aspects of awakening, five wisdoms, seed syllable, charnel ground, eight yoginīs, Gaurī, completion stage, mandala, Derge Tengyur</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the commentary is glossing a verse on the supernatural knowledges</meta>
...it is knowing the minds of oneself and others in the past, the future, and the present.

On the passage beginning "In the heavens and in the human realm": "a single form" means a single nature. The meaning of the passage beginning "the portion of self and other" has already been explained.

In order to show that Hevajra is superior to other scriptures, the text says "All the Vedas" and so on. The <term>Vedas</term> <gloss>the sacred scriptures of the brahmins</gloss> are the four: the Veda of verses of praise, the Veda of protection, the Veda of chants, and the Veda of sacrifice. <note>The Tibetan names appear to correspond to the Ṛgveda, Atharvaveda, Sāmaveda, and Yajurveda.</note> The "philosophical systems" are the views held by non-Buddhist teachers, such as the <term>Purāṇas</term> <gloss>"ancient" lore</gloss>, and also the sūtras and so on of the <term>Śrāvaka</term> <gloss>"Hearer," disciples of the early Buddhist path</gloss> canon, so called because by them one comes to put an end to rebirth. "Ritual expansion" refers to the Kriyā tantras and the like. In none of these is there accomplishment of the kind that has been described here.

If one asks whether such accomplishment exists in the Perfection Vehicle or not, the text says "Existence becomes pure" and so on. "Purity" means the path whose character is the six perfections, called pure because it exhausts the obscurations of the afflictions and the obscurations to the knowable. By this purity one does attain awakening; however, "at the end of existence" means after passing from one birth to the next for three countless aeons.

Now, if it is said that in the Yoga tantras, too, awakening is attained in this very life, then in what way is this teaching superior to them? To this the text says "Without it as well" and so on. "It" means the <term>sahaja</term> <gloss>the innate, coemergent bliss</gloss>, whose character is self-awareness. Without it, accomplishment is not said to exist either in this life or in any other life.

If so, what is the difference between that and this? The text says "Whoever does not know Hevajra" and so on. In other tantras the innate is merely indicated, but in this Hevajra it is taught in a fully clarified form. Therefore it is shown very clearly that for whoever does not know Hevajra, the labor of study, reflection, and meditation becomes meaningless.

If...

<summary>The commentary explains a passage of the Hevajra Tantra asserting its superiority over the Vedas, non-Buddhist systems, the Śrāvaka sūtras, the Kriyā tantras, the Perfection Vehicle, and even the Yoga tantras. The key is the innate bliss of self-awareness, which other tantras only hint at but Hevajra teaches clearly.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, commentary, Vedas, Purāṇas, Śrāvaka, Kriyā tantra, Yoga tantra, Perfection Vehicle, six perfections, three countless aeons, sahaja, innate bliss, self-awareness, two obscurations, superiority of Hevajra</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the commentary is distinguishing the worldly innate bliss, used as an example, from the great bliss that is to be accomplished</meta>
...since it is to be established through the example by which it becomes similar, that very thing is what is taught as primary, while this is only a figurative designation. To show this, the text says "Like a lamp in the darkness" and so on. Just as one shows that pots, cloth, and other things lying in a dark place are made visible by a lamp, so too it should be understood that the worldly innate bliss, which serves as the example <note>the woodblock reading is uncertain between "print" and "example"; "example" fits the sense</note>, brings about great bliss, whose character is that which is to be accomplished.

On the passage beginning "In the abode of bliss," in order to make clear what was said before, the text says "Thirty-two" and so on. This refers to the body blazing with the major marks and minor signs. <note>The thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs are the bodily characteristics of a buddha.</note> "The Lord" means the master of the qualities of a buddha. "The consort" is the example, namely the vajra consort. "The seminal fluid in her <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>womb, the female organ</gloss>" means that he himself abides there. The fluid is bliss, that is, the external fluid. "Without it" means if that fluid is absent. This is because bliss arises in dependence on the fluid; without the fluid, no other cause is able to produce such bliss.

For this reason it is said that bliss also arises from deity yoga. In the same way, one who desires great bliss must certainly practice deity yoga. Its path is neither an entity nor a non-entity, because it is of the very nature of fluid and bliss. The Buddha who is its fruit is likewise neither an entity nor a non-entity.

How is this so? The text says "Faces and arms in form" and so on. In its nature as the <term>sambhogakāya</term> <gloss>body of perfect enjoyment</gloss>, the Buddha has form. As the <term>dharmakāya</term> <gloss>body of reality</gloss> of supreme bliss, it is formless. Therefore, since it has a form that does not abide, it does not abide in the statement "It is neither with form nor formless." Because this is so, the text says "Therefore all beings are innate," that is, all sentient beings. The innate...

<summary>The commentary explains how worldly innate bliss serves as an example that illuminates great bliss, like a lamp lighting objects in the dark. It then glosses verses on the Lord and his consort, the role of the seminal fluid in giving rise to bliss, the necessity of deity yoga, and the Buddha as both formed (sambhogakāya) and formless (dharmakāya).</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, commentary, innate bliss, great bliss, lamp analogy, thirty-two marks, vajra consort, bhaga, seminal fluid, deity yoga, entity and non-entity, sambhogakāya, dharmakāya, sahaja, all beings innate</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the end of a quoted verse, followed by the commentator's discussion of whether meditation is needed to realize the innate</meta>
"...will become." Thus meditation is not pointless, because without the complete perfection of meditation one is unable to make it directly manifest. As it is also said:

The path that draws out
The thorn of existence I have shown to you.
The Tathāgatas are only teachers;
You yourselves must strive with diligence.

<note>This verse echoes a well-known saying of the Buddha: the Tathāgatas only point the way, and the effort must be one's own.</note>

Someone objects: "If that is so of the transcendent path, then the joy of the innate is directly perceived by all who engage in sensual pleasure. If even instruction about it is pointless, what need is there to speak of meditation? What can another's instruction do for something that is directly perceived?" In reply the text says "Merit" and so on.

The intention is this. Here the worldly joy of the innate is not what is to be accomplished, since it is already established. It is inferior to the bliss of the god realms and the higher realms in ascending order, and because it is tainted it is a stain; therefore it is the root of the faults of those who wander in <term>saṃsāra</term> <gloss>the cycle of rebirth</gloss>.

What, then, is to be accomplished? The individual discerning knowledge of the Tathāgatas, which is the innate <term>dharmakāya</term> <gloss>body of reality</gloss>, like space; and the <term>sambhogakāya</term> <gloss>body of perfect enjoyment</gloss> that arises in accord with it as its corresponding result. That innate, supremely excellent, utterly pure, whose character is certain bliss: that is what is to be accomplished here.

This is not realized by any other means. Through meditation on the worldly joy of the innate itself, with heightened devotion to the instruction just as it was given, the perfection of meditation becomes manifest and one knows it oneself. It is not so from the very beginning. Therefore the meaning is that here study, reflection, and meditation are not pointless.

"The means" is the path. "Relying on it" is correct meditation. "Its many lineages" means "many kinds." "Obtained from the guru" refers to the guru's proper occasion: the guru should bestow it according to the rite upon a suitable disciple in whom the lineage has gone before, which means that he imparts the oral instructions. That which is to be realized...

<summary>The commentary argues that study, reflection, and meditation are not pointless even though worldly innate joy is directly experienced in sexual pleasure. That worldly joy is tainted and inferior; what must be accomplished is the pure innate dharmakāya and its sambhogakāya, realized only through meditation on the guru's instructions given according to the rite.</summary>
<keywords>Hevajra Tantra, commentary, innate joy, sahaja, meditation, Tathāgata, worldly bliss, tainted bliss, dharmakāya, sambhogakāya, discerning knowledge, guru, oral instructions, lineage, study reflection and meditation</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the commentary is discussing the thirty-two channels of the subtle body</meta>
...is merely a number. It is not an explanation of a number that depends on the petals of a lotus, because there is no statement saying "the number depending on the petals," and because the text also speaks of "the channel in the center of the lotus at the heart."

Among these, the one in which <term>Akṣobhya</term> <gloss>the "Immovable" buddha, here standing for semen</gloss> flows is the <term>lalanā</term> <gloss>the left channel</gloss>. From the <term>rasanā</term> <gloss>the right channel</gloss> it is chiefly blood that flows. This is what is meant by the passage beginning "Among them."

"Having the nature of wisdom" means that chiefly the moon flows there. "Of method" means having the nature of method, that is, it is where blood flows. "That very thing" means the Buddha. And from what does it come that it is also formless? The answer is "supreme bliss": the meaning is that it is so also because the dharmakāya enjoys the bliss of the Dharma. For that very reason the fruit is neither an entity nor a non-entity.

Therefore all beings are the joy of the innate; that innate is connected with the innate of the Buddha himself. "All beings" means all sentient beings. To the thought, "Why is it called 'innate through buddhahood itself'?", the text says, "Innate," and so on. Its nature is its very essence, and so the text speaks this way. Its nature is <term>nirvāṇa</term> <gloss>the state beyond sorrow</gloss>: the pure nature is that, and mind too is that. The intention is this: because in the ultimate sense it is pure and has passed beyond sorrow, it is not an entity; and because mind itself is of the nature of purity, it is not a non-entity either. Someone may object: "In that case the sambhogakāya would have no seed. The ordinary body belongs to that ordinary body itself, and it is of a different kind from the divine body." Therefore the text says, "Of the deity," and so on. Here too, by the words "the form of the deity," its very seed is taught.

<meta>continues from previous page; final folio of Vasubandhu's commentary on the Noble Sūtra of the Four Factors <note>Sanskrit: <term>Āryacaturdharmakanirdeśa</term></note></meta>The words "one should not give them up as long as one lives" show that these factors must be practised continuously. The words "even for the sake of one's life" show that they must be practised with respect.

Why are they called "the four factors," neither fewer nor more? Because there are four factors that obstruct the accumulations for awakening, and these four are their remedies.

What are the four obstructing factors? Not seeking the goal; not knowing the means; not being turned toward beings; and being turned toward sense objects. Again, there are four: not undertaking; undertaking wrongly; abandoning what one has undertaken; and being distracted in what one has undertaken.

Again, there are four factors that are conducive to the accumulations for awakening. They are four because they are the basis of those accumulations. What are the four factors conducive to the accumulations for awakening? Wanting instruction and further teaching; obtaining it; being a vessel for it; and accomplishing it.

Again, there are four: seeking the goal; knowing the means; and practice. Here practice is of two kinds: bringing beings to maturity, and bringing the qualities of a buddha to maturity. Again, there are four: not abandoning cyclic existence <note>Tibetan: 'khor ba, Sanskrit <term>saṃsāra</term></note>; being free of affliction while within it; gathering beings; and having trained in diligence.

Again, it is through four causes that one crosses a path that is hard to travel: wishing to go; knowing the way; not losing heart and giving up; and being careful <note>Tibetan: bag yod pa, conscientiousness or heedfulness</note>. In the same way one crosses the path of cyclic existence. They are four because they are the basis of these.

Why is someone who strives earnestly for the awakening of the hearers <note><term>śrāvakas</term> <gloss>disciples who seek personal liberation</gloss></note> or of the solitary buddhas <note><term>pratyekabuddhas</term> <gloss>those who awaken on their own without teaching others</gloss></note> not called a bodhisattva? Because the name is established for the unsurpassed alone, just as with "the illuminator." <note>The term "illuminator" (snang byed) is reserved for the sun, though lamps and the moon also give light; in the same way "bodhisattva" is reserved for one aiming at unsurpassed awakening.</note>

To sum up the meaning: in this sūtra the Blessed One has fully taught the actions that are suited to those who have rightly entered the Great Vehicle <note><term>Mahāyāna</term></note>, and how those actions do not remain without their fruit.

The Explanation of the Noble Four Factors, composed by the master Vasubandhu, is complete.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>At that time, the aspect that abides as one's own inexpressible, nonconceptual nature is called "the form that is the true nature of phenomena" <term>dharmatā-rūpa</term> <gloss>form as reality itself</gloss>. "Maitreya, imagined form should be regarded as not substantially existent": this is because it is utterly nonexistent.

"Conceptualized form should be regarded as substantially existent, because conceptualization exists substantially": it exists because it exists conventionally. "But it does not function independently": this is said because it has a dependent nature <term>paratantra</term> <gloss>the nature of arising in dependence on other causes</gloss>.

"The form that is the true nature of phenomena is neither not substantially existent nor substantially existent." Since it does not exist in the aspect of a conceptualized entity, it cannot be said "it exists" either; therefore it is not "substantially existent."
